Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the Apex Power Generation third quarter 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. To ask a question, you will need to register by pressing star one one. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Thompson, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson: Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Apex Power Generation's third quarter 2024 Earnings Call. Joining me on the call today are David Harlan, Chief Executive Officer; Emily Vargas, Chief Financial Officer; and Robert Kline, Chief Operating Officer.

Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that statements made during this call that are not historical facts are forward-looking statements and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from those expressed or implied. Please refer to our SEC filings for a detailed discussion of these risks.

Now, I'll turn the call over to David Harlan.

David Harlan: Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to report on our performance this quarter. We continued to execute on our strategic priorities, delivering solid results in a challenging environment.

Our performance was driven by strong operational performance in our generation fleet, continued growth in our renewable energy portfolio, effective cost management, and progress on our infrastructure investments.

Let me provide some more detail on these four key aspects. First, our generation fleet demonstrated exceptional reliability, with overall availability exceeding 94 percent across our thermal and nuclear assets. We minimized unplanned outages through advanced predictive maintenance and digital monitoring systems, which allowed us to meet peak demand efficiently even amidst variable weather patterns and grid stresses.

Second, our renewable portfolio saw meaningful expansion, with 450 megawatts of solar-plus-storage projects reaching commercial operation under long-term power purchase agreements. This builds on our 1.2-gigawatt development pipeline, positioning us to capitalize on rising demand from data centers and electrification trends.

Third, we maintained tight control over costs, holding operations and maintenance expenses to a modest two percent increase year-over-year. This was achieved through synergies from recent acquisitions, optimized fuel hedging, and operational efficiencies that kept us below budget.

Fourth, our infrastructure investments advanced steadily, with significant progress on transmission upgrades and grid hardening projects that enhance reliability and support renewable integrations. These efforts are laying the groundwork for sustained growth.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Emily to discuss the financials.

Emily Vargas: Thank you, David. Good morning, everyone. For the third quarter, we reported adjusted earnings per share of $1.62 and revenue of $2.8 billion. Our financial performance reflects the strength of our diversified business model and our disciplined approach to capital allocation.

Our capital expenditure for the quarter was $825 million, primarily focused on renewable energy developments, transmission reconductoring, and battery storage deployments. We remain committed to maintaining a strong balance sheet and returning value to shareholders.

To elaborate on our earnings per share performance, which came in strong this quarter and highlights the resilience of our diversified portfolio spanning regulated utilities, competitive power generation, and renewables, let's break it down. On a GAAP basis, diluted EPS reached $1.47, a 12 percent increase from $1.31 in the third quarter of 2023, reflecting solid execution tempered by some non-recurring items. Our adjusted EPS, excluding one-time charges from the early retirement of our final coal unit at Riverbend and mark-to-market losses on financial transmission rights in PJM, hit $1.62—beating the midpoint of our $1.55 to $1.60 guidance and up eight percent from $1.50 last year. Over the trailing twelve months, adjusted EPS is now $5.95, keeping us on pace for full-year 2024 guidance of $6.10 to $6.30.

Key drivers included robust commercial and industrial load growth, which accounted for about 45 percent of the EPS upside. Electricity demand in our Northeast regulated areas jumped 6.5 percent year-over-year, propelled by hyperscale data centers from customers like Amazon Web Services and Microsoft. In PJM, with our substantial 12-gigawatt regulated fleet, load factors averaged 72 percent, up from 68 percent, thanks to AI computing demands. This added roughly $0.08 per share via higher retail rates under formula mechanisms, akin to trends at Dominion Energy and Exelon. In ERCOT, our merchant gas peakers seized real-time prices averaging $85 per megawatt-hour during summer peaks, contributing another $0.05.

Our renewables segment exceeded forecasts, adding $0.12 per share. We commissioned 450 megawatts of solar-plus-storage in the Southeast with long-term PPAs from investment-grade buyers, delivering a 25-year levelized cost of energy near $35 per megawatt-hour, in line with NextEra's FPL bids. Wind fleet capacity factors in MISO rose to 38 percent on better wind patterns, while our 300-megawatt BESS in California profited from 15 percent arbitrage in net peak events under resource adequacy markets. EBITDA margins there climbed to 65 percent, a 300 basis point gain, aided by $50 million in extended PTC and ITC benefits from the Inflation Reduction Act.

Cost discipline and efficiencies added a $0.07 tailwind. O&M rose just two percent to $420 million, under plan, via digital twin tech at nuclear sites like Three Rivers, cutting forced outages below one percent—matching Entergy benchmarks. Fuel for CCGT came in at $2.45 per million Btu, 10 percent under Henry Hub, with 85 percent hedged for 2024. We captured $30 million in synergies from our Texas acquisition, streamlining dispatch over 1.8 gigawatts of gas assets.

Regionally, Northeast regulated operations—65 percent of earnings—gained from hotter weather, with 1,200 cooling degree days versus a normal 1,050, lifting residential use four percent. Midwest merchant faced mild hydro in MISO, offset by BRA 2025 capacity wins at $250 per kilowatt-year for two gigawatts, securing $0.04 per share.

Headwinds totaled about $0.10 per share: interest costs up from refinancing $1.2 billion at 5.2 percent versus prior 3.8 percent, costing $0.06 amid broader rate pressures like at Southern Company; 15 percent transformer cost hikes delayed $20 million capex recoveries; and FERC ROE tweaks cut 25 basis points in PJM, though we're appealing.

These outcomes affirm our "Powering the Energy Transition" strategy, accelerating net-zero with 1.2 gigawatts of new renewables and BESS in 2025 for 40 percent clean unforced capacity. Highlights include hydrogen blending at Susquehanna NGCC targeting 20 percent by 2026 with DOE funding, and virtual power plants aggregating 50 megawatts residential DERs with Tesla's Autobidder, eyeing $2-3 billion IRA opportunities like Avangrid's wind.

Q4 adjusted EPS guides to $1.70-$1.80, full-year reaffirmed at $6.10-$6.30. Watch gas volatility—2025 hedges at $3.10 per million Btu—and RPS risks in Illinois, but 85 percent locked generation bolsters us.

Shifting to rate base growth, a key pillar of our earnings stability in this regulated landscape, our consolidated rate base hit $28.4 billion as of September 30, up 6.8 percent year-over-year and ahead of our 5-7 percent full-year target. This extends 12 straight quarters of strong additions from our $3.2 billion 2024 capex program.

Rate base—mainly net utility plant, CWIP, and working capital—underpins our 9.75 percent average authorized ROE post-Midwest and Southeast settlements. Year-to-date, $1.8 billion in new investments entered rate base, yielding $175 million incremental revenue at blended ROE, plus 45 basis points AFUDC.

By segment: Generation grew 9.2 percent to $11.2 billion, or 42 percent of YTD growth, driven by IRA credits and data center demand. We energized 450 megawatts Southeast solar, like 250-megawatt Pine Ridge in Georgia with full ITC and 15-year PPA from a cloud giant like Microsoft. BESS shone with 300 megawatts in Texas and Midwest, such as 150-megawatt Horizon paired with peakers for ERCOT. These earn over seven percent AFUDC, adding $0.12 EPS YTD. Next, 1.2 gigawatts offshore wind off Carolinas eyes Q2 2025 FERC nod, with BOEM delays shifting $200 million to CWIP.

Transmission surged 8.5 percent to $7.9 billion, 35 percent of growth, via MISO/PJM incentives for high-voltage. $850 million capex covers 200 miles 345 kV reconductoring, cutting losses 15 percent and enabling 500 megawatts renewables. Midwest AI data centers swelled our queue to 15 gigawatts, like NextEra's, spurring $1.5 billion expansions by 2027. Full CWIP in Illinois at 10.25 percent ROE, but 25 percent YoY transformer inflation trimmed ROE 20 basis points.

Distribution rose 5.1 percent to $9.3 billion, 23 percent of growth, from 2.1 percent load growth topping national 1.5 percent via 18 percent EV uptake in Southeast and manufacturing like Ford's Tennessee gigafactory adding 150 megawatts peak. $400 million AMI 2.0 with DERMS for solar/EV mirrors Duke Energy, improving FLISR outages 22 percent. California wildfire caps hit adjacent, but East focus protects.

For 2024, rate base eyes 6.5 percent growth with $3.4-3.6 billion capex at 95 percent equity recovery. Enablers: three $450 million revenue dockets, 80 percent hedged construction at SOFR +125 bps. Risks: 4-6 percent 2025 steel/labor inflation, FERC Order 1920, queue delays deferring $800 million renewables. Mitigants: $2 billion green credit facility, 50/50 BESS JV with infrastructure fund.

This rate base path cements our "power renaissance" lead—from IRA renewables to AI demand—with 6-8 percent CAGR delivering 80 percent regulated earnings growth through the decade.

Before outlining forward-looking guidance, let me reiterate that all statements today on expectations, plans, and projections are forward-looking under the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. They're based on current views but face risks like natural gas price swings, RTO interconnection delays in PJM and MISO, shifting FERC transmission policies under Order 1920, supply chain issues for high-voltage transformers and bifacial solar modules, interest rate shifts on our $2.5 billion revolver, SCADA cyber threats, and regulatory shifts such as IRA credit changes like 45X PTC for solar/wind or 48E ITC for storage. See our 10-K and 10-Q for full risks.

For full-year 2025, we guide consolidated adjusted EBITDA to $1.85-$1.95 billion, eight to 12 percent above 2024's $1.72 billion midpoint, led by Generation's six to eight percent revenue rise to $3.2-$3.4 billion from higher ERCOT spark spreads—$28 per megawatt-hour Q3 on 2.8-gigawatt gas fleet—and 1.2-gigawatt renewables online. AFFO at $1.45-$1.55 per share, seven to 10 percent EPS growth, with 55-60 percent payout on six percent dividend hike to $1.92 annual.

Renewables: 25 percent EBITDA CAGR to $650 million by 2028 from $420 million, backed by 1,500 megawatts solar/wind exiting construction 2025-2026—like 450-megawatt Desert Bloom PV in CAISO at 12.5 percent IRR, fully permitted, and 300-megawatt Windridge II hybrid in SPP with 150-megawatt/600-megawatt-hour BESS. 85 percent backlog in 15-year PPAs at $42 per megawatt-hour average, 40 percent hyperscalers like Microsoft/Google amid data center boom—12 gigawatts by 2030 in PJM/ERCOT/MISO per EIA, $1.2 billion revenue potential at 90 percent factors.

Thermal: 5.2-gigawatt CCGT/coal-gas fleet steady at $750-$800 million EBITDA, ERCOT merchant 15-18 percent ROIC as heat rates hit 7,500 Btu/kWh with peaker exits. CCUS on two 800-megawatt Heartland units targets 90 percent CO2 capture for $50/ton 45Q credits, $120 million yearly post-2027. Nuclear uprate 1,100 megawatts at Palisades Unit 2 follows Vistra, $200 per megawatt-hour MISO spreads, Q4 2026 restart with $1.5 billion DOE loan.

Transmission: $1.1 billion of $2.8 billion FY25 capex—55 percent—to 500 kV PJM reconductoring for 2.5x ROI via formula rates, including $450 million Tri-State HVDC easing 3-gigawatt constraints, aiding 800 megawatts batteries. 4.2-gigawatt queues, 70 percent Phase II, $300 million ERCOT prepay.

Pillars: Electrification resilience via $500 million grid-edge microgrids/VPPs with Stem/AutoGrid for 200 megawatts DERs; decarbonization to 60 percent carbon-free by 2030 with NuScale VOYGR-12 SMRs for 462-megawatt Texas site, 20 percent hydrogen gas pilots; capital efficiency at 18-20 percent FFO/debt, $800 million rotations like coal sales to NRG.

ERCOT 4.5 percent load CAGR to 2028 per SARA boosts 3-gigawatt portfolio; PJM auctions at $100/kW-year aid 1.5-gigawatt peakers; CAISO storage 95 percent efficiency nets $150/kW-month ancillaries. UK Hornsea 4 offshore 20 percent stake (2.4 gigawatts 2029) hedges at £55/megawatt-hour CfDs.

Outlook assumes conservative gas $3.50/MMBtu, solar $0.28/watt DC, 5.5 percent 10-year Treasury—but data center PPAs/IRA transferability could lift EBITDA 15 percent+. Positioned for 9-11 percent dividend growth, superior TSR.

David Harlan: Thank you, Emily. Now, we'll open the line for questions.

Operator: Thank you. Our first question comes from Mike Ross with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Mike Ross: Good morning, team. Can you elaborate on your plans for renewables expansion, particularly data center PPAs?

David Harlan: Certainly, Mike. Our renewables platform is a core growth driver, with a 25 percent EBITDA CAGR targeted through 2028. We've locked 85 percent of our 1,500-megawatt backlog into 15-year PPAs at $42 per megawatt-hour, including significant hyperscaler exposure—40 percent of new additions from Microsoft and Google equivalents. Data center loads in PJM, ERCOT, and MISO could add 12 gigawatts by 2030, unlocking $1.2 billion revenue at high capacity factors. Projects like Desert Bloom and Windridge II exemplify this, blending solar, wind, and BESS for optimal dispatch.

Operator: Our next question comes from Lisa Chen with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Lisa Chen: Thanks. What is your outlook for rate base growth into 2025?

Emily Vargas: Good question, Lisa. We're tracking toward six to eight percent CAGR through the decade, building on this year's 6.5 percent. Key drivers include $3.4 to $3.6 billion capex fully recovered, proactive rate cases for $450 million new revenues, and transmission incentives under FERC reforms. While inflation and queues pose risks, our CWIP recoveries and partnerships mitigate, ensuring 80 percent regulated earnings growth.

Operator: Our next question comes from Tom Baker with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Tom Baker: Morning. How are you mitigating supply chain risks for major capex projects?

Robert Kline: Hi Tom. Supply chain remains a focus, especially transformers and modules. We've prepaid $300 million to ERCOT for faster interconnections, hedged 80 percent construction costs, and partnered on JVs like our BESS fund tie-up. Digital tools and diversified sourcing—from U.S. to allies—keep delays minimal, with contingency buffers in our $2.8 billion FY25 plan.

Operator: There are no further questions at this time. I would like to turn the call back over to David Harlan for closing remarks.

David Harlan: Thank you. In summary, we delivered solid results in the third quarter 2024, demonstrating the strength of our business model and our commitment to creating long-term value for our shareholders. We remain focused on executing our strategic priorities and positioning Apex Power Generation for continued success. Thank you for your time and interest in Apex Power Generation.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
